y-m-45-01.s.s1.r.b: Maybe you think opposite slope signs enough. Multiply slopes direct.
y-m-45-01.s.s1.r.c: Vertical and horizontal line slopes hard to describe, so easy to miss. Picture angle in drawing.
y-m-45-01.s.s1.r.d: For general form, find slope first, then check product. Rearrange for y.
y-m-45-01.s.s1.explain: For (가), slopes 2 and −1/2 multiply to −1; for (라), slopes −3/2 and 2/3 also give −1, so perpendicular. (다) vertical and horizontal, also perpendicular. (나) slopes 3,−3 give −9, so not perpendicular.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.prompt: Using (가) to (라) evidence, judge 민재 statement.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.hint.0: First check if slope product can be found for each perpendicular pair in table.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.hint.1: If one perpendicular pair has no computable product, check how it affects statement.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.o.a: False. (다) perpendicular but slope product cannot be found, so statement not right as written.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.r.a: You use (다) as counterexample and call statement false. One counterexample is good; now consider range where true.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.o.b: True. For perpendicular pairs (가),(라), product −1, so I think always true.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.r.b: Two fitting examples no prove ‘always’. Check for a table pair that fails.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.o.c: True only for lines with slopes. Pairs including vertical line need separate handling.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.r.c: If restricted to lines with defined slopes, statement true. You state its range.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.o.d: Cannot judge until more lines tested.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.r.d: One example can disprove ‘always’. Check table for such one.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.explain: For lines whose slopes defined (neither vertical), if perpendicular, product −1. If vertical line included like (다), slope undefined, so no product to discuss. So false as written or true only when slopes exist are both reasonable.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.acc.0: If claim means ‘all perpendicular pairs’, (다) is example where it fails as written, so calling false reasonable. Better also say range where it is true.

y-m-45-01.s.s3.explain: Slope of 2x+3y=6 is −2/3, so perpendicular slope 3/2; coefficients (p,q) are multiple of (3,−2). Examples 3x−2y+1=0, 3x−2y−4=0. 6x−4y+2=0 is same as 3x−2y+1=0.

y-m-45-05.prereq.0: H2 only production difficulty, not school grade. Assume learner studied middle-school linear functions/slope and Pythagorean theorem, and high-school line equations.
y-m-45-05.title: When does upward-moving line leave circle?
y-m-45-05.goal: Use data to predict intersection count as y-intercept rises; refine tangency guess into calculation.
y-m-45-05.material: Circle C:x²+y²=25 (center 0, radius 5), line y=x+k (y-intercept k, slope 1). Increase k from 0 and track intersections. √2 read root 2, about 1.414. [25 5 1 0 2 2 1.414]
y-m-45-05.s.s1.prompt: Data revealed stepwise; predict and revise.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.hint.0: At each step check if new data conflicts with earlier prediction.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.hint.1: Choose k and substitute into x²+(x+k)²=25 to count intersections. [25]
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.info: k=0 gives y=x through center, so two intersections. [0]
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: As k increases from 0, how many intersections do you expect? [0]
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.after: k=0 alone cannot tell tangency point. Both guesses a,c worth testing. [0]
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: E stay 2 for some time, then at one point become 1 (tangent), after that become 0.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Correct direction to think tangency go happen. We no know when yet.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: As soon as k positive small, it become 1 straight, then stay 0.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Line wey pass circle center only move small. E no go far enough to touch tangent immediately.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Tangent at k=5 (y-intercept equal radius), then become 0.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Na idea say tangent when y-intercept equal radius. Guess worth testing.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: That mean even if line go far up, e still meet circle. Remember circle occupy small area.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Test k=5. Put y=x+5 in x²+y²=25: x²+(x+5)²=25, so 2x²+10x=0, hence x=0 or −5. Meeting points na (0,5), (−5,0). 5 5 25 5 25 2 10 0 0 5 0 5 5 0
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: At k=5 line no tangent; e meet circle at 2 points. Which judgment fit positive k value where tangent happen?
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.after: Although y-intercept equal radius 5, no tangent. Slope 1 makes line cross circle slantwise; tangency happen higher up.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: If tangent at k<5, at k=5 line should no longer meet. But k=5 get 2 points.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Check calculation again. (0,5) and (−5,0) both lie on circle. 0 5 5 0
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: k=5 still give 2 points, so tangency appears at higher value.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Circle has limited size, so if line go high enough, e no meet. Tangency happen somewhere between.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: At k=8, how many intersection points fit?
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.after: It could be 2 or 0 depending if tangent k above or below 8. Calculate generally.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Data so far no decide, because tangent k may be above or below 8.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This judgment say exactly what data cannot decide.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It go be 2, because tangent k fit higher than 8.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Up to k=7, two points; possible, but not settled.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Up to k=7, two points; possible, but not settled.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Exactly 1, pattern suggest tangent happen at 8.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: No data show tangent at 8. You assume a lucky guess.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It go be 0 because tangent k fit between 7 and 8.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.info: Substitute y=x+k into circle equation: 2x²+2kx+k²−25=0. One-quarter discriminant na k²−2(k²−25)=50−k². Positive means two points; 0 tangent; negative no meeting. √50=5√2≈7.07.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.ask: For which k range line meet circle at 2 different points?
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.after: Tangency at k=5√2 (about 7.07) and k=−5√2. At k=8, no intersection. First guess ‘tangent when y-intercept equal radius’ wrong because line slope 1. 5 2 7 07 5 2 8 0 1
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.r.b: At k=5 and 7 they still meet twice. Test guess say 5 is endpoint.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.r.c: k=7 gives 2 points; 7.05 also fit give 2. Find exact endpoint.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.o.d: All k less than 5√2, even very small negative values.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.r.d: Think about very small negative k. Line far below circle.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.reflect: If you first guessed tangent at k=5, how data showing 2 points there change guess? What prediction did 2 points at k=7 allow, and wetin still open? Separate waiting for hidden info from testing guess with calculation. 5 5 7
y-m-45-05.s.s2.prompt: Instead of discriminant, find same range by comparing distance from circle center to line with radius. Center (0,0) to x−y+k=0 distance |k|/√2. Which comparison correct? 0 0 0 2
y-m-45-05.s.s2.hint.0: First compare center-line distance and intersection count at k=0.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.o.a: If distance >5, they meet at 2 points; equal means tangent; less means no meeting.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.r.a: When distance big, line move away. You reverse ‘greater’ and ‘less.’
y-m-45-05.s.s2.o.b: Treat distance as k and say tangent when k=5.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.r.b: k only y-intercept, not perpendicular distance from center to line. With slope 1, these lengths differ.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.o.c: If distance |k|/√2 <5, two intersections; equal tangent; >5 no meeting.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.r.c: Distance-vs-radius comparison gives same result: close means they meet, far means no.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.o.d: Distance formula only works when no circle? For circle use only discriminant.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.r.d: Point-to-line distance formula exists, so use distance.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.explain: If distance |k|/√2 is less than radius 5, there are 2 points. |k|<5√2, same as −5√2<k<5√2 from discriminant. Both methods match.

y-m-45-06.title: Does checking with one number set prove it?
y-m-45-06.topic: Coordinate choice and generality when proving figure property with coordinates
y-m-45-06.goal: When coordinate-proof of figure property, choose setup representing every triangle, and tell friend why special example alone no prove general result.
y-m-45-06.material: M,N are midpoints of sides AB and AC in triangle ABC. Prove with coordinates MN parallel BC and length half BC. (√3 read ‘root 3’.) Coordinate placement matters.
y-m-45-06.thinking.0: Choose coordinate arrangement without losing generality
y-m-45-06.thinking.2: Fix it and explain to friend clearly
y-m-45-06.prereq.1: Midpoint, slope, and distance between points
y-m-45-06.prereq.2: Known middle-school fact about segment joining triangle side midpoints
y-m-45-06.s.s1.prompt: You want prove fact for any triangle ABC. Choose all coordinate setups able represent every triangle (no loss of generality). a,b,c letters no shape restriction, like positive numbers.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each setup, see what triangle shapes possible by changing vertex coordinates.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.hint.1: With each setup, test if you can make right, equilateral, and arbitrary triangles.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.o.a: A(0,0), B(4,0), C(0,3) (all coordinates fixed numbers) 0 0 4 0 0 3
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.a: Fixed numbers show only one right triangle.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.b: If one side lies on x-axis and one vertex origin, remaining vertex free, so any triangle possible.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.c: It fixes A x-coordinate at 0, so only triangles with right angle at B.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.d: Only one equilateral triangle with all sides 2.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.e: This put midpoint of BC at origin. A is free, so any triangle possible.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.f: It puts A on perpendicular bisector of BC, so only isosceles triangles.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.explain: Translate/rotate triangle so one side on x-axis (flip if needed so A above), and one vertex at origin, or midpoint of side at origin. Movement no change lengths or parallel lines, so b and e represent any triangle. a,c,d,f only fixed-shape triangles like right, equilateral, isosceles.
y-m-45-06.s.s2.prompt: A student set A(0,0), B(4,0), C(0,3) and wrote below. Choose proof line that is problem (one line enough). 0 0 4 0 0 3
y-m-45-06.s.s2.hint.0: Recalculate lines 2–4 one by one; check if correct for this triangle.
y-m-45-06.s.s2.hint.1: Compare triangles possible under line 1 coordinates with range line 5 claims.
y-m-45-06.s.s2.line.0: Set ABC vertices A(0,0), B(4,0), C(0,3). 0 0 4 0 0 3
y-m-45-06.s.s2.line.1: AB midpoint M=(2,0), AC midpoint N=(0,3/2). 2 0 0 3 2
y-m-45-06.s.s2.line.3: MN=√(2²+(3/2)²)=5/2; BC=√(4²+3²)=5, so MN half BC.
y-m-45-06.s.s2.line.4: Therefore for every triangle, segment joining two side midpoints is parallel to third side and half its length.
y-m-45-06.s.s2.explain: Lines 1 and 5 are problem. Calculations 2–4 correct, but line 1 fixed coordinates to one right triangle, so cannot claim ‘every triangle’ in line 5. Only this triangle tested.
y-m-45-06.s.s3.prompt: Tell friend why this no prove all triangles and write 2–3 sentences how to fix it. Use easy words.
y-m-45-06.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine explaining to friend; first say what type triangle this solution dealt with.
y-m-45-06.s.s3.hint.1: Remember how to write coordinates to include other triangle shapes too.
y-m-45-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: This solution is ... so ... To fix it ...
y-m-45-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You explain reason concretely so friend understand?
y-m-45-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You say ‘it does not represent every triangle’ instead of ‘calculation wrong’?
y-m-45-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You check your fix really include every triangle?
y-m-45-06.s.s3.model.0: A(0,0), B(4,0), C(0,3) is just one right triangle. We no know if it works for other shapes. Use letters e.g. B(0,0), C(c,0), A(a,b), then repeat calculation.
y-m-45-06.s.s3.model.1: One number set only checks non-right cases? Actually it misses them. Use arbitrary a,b,c coordinates so triangle can be any shape.

y-m-45-08.title: If move order change, result same?
y-m-45-08.topic: Order when combining translation and reflection
y-m-45-08.goal: Find error in line-movement solution; find/generalize when changing order of translation and reflection across y=x gives same result.
y-m-45-08.material: Move line m: y=2x+1 twice. ㉠ translate 3 in x direction (3 right); ㉡ reflect across y=x. 지후 do ㉠ then ㉡.
y-m-45-08.thinking.1: Make cases where order can swap
y-m-45-08.prereq.1: Translating figure (replace x with x−a, y with y−b)
y-m-45-08.prereq.2: Reflection in y=x swaps x and y
y-m-45-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose first wrong line in Jihu solution. 지후
y-m-45-08.s.s1.hint.0: Pick point on translated line and reverse to original point.
y-m-45-08.s.s1.hint.1: Point (0,1) on m; check where it moves 3 right. [0 1 3]
y-m-45-08.s.s1.line.0: Translate m right 3: substitute x−3: y=2(x−3)+1=2x−5. [3 3 2 3 1 2 7]
y-m-45-08.s.s1.line.1: Reflect about y=x: swap x,y, so x=2y−5. [2 7]
y-m-45-08.s.s1.explain: Line 1 wrong. Point (x,y) moves right 3 to (x+3,y), so substitute x−3: y=2(x−3)+1=2x−5. Later lines carry error. Correct result y=(x+5)/2 from x=2y−5. [1 3 3 3 2 3 1 2 5 1 5 2 2 5]
y-m-45-08.s.s2.prompt: For point (1,3), find 3 nonzero (p,q) where translate by (p,q), then reflect y=x, equals reflect first then translate. (p,q) means horizontal, vertical move. [1 3 1 3 0 0]
y-m-45-08.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate final coordinates for both orders using p,q. [1 3]
y-m-45-08.s.s2.hint.1: Equate final x and y coordinates; find relation between p,q.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Find coordinates for both orders, compare x and y.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.explain: Translate then reflect: (1+p,3+q)→(3+q,1+p). Reflect then translate: (3,1)→(3+p,1+q). Equality requires p=q. Examples (1,1),(2,2),(−3,−3). [1 3 3 1 3 1 3 1 3 3 1 1 1 1 2 2 3 3]
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.prompt: State common feature of your (p,q), explain why swapping order preserves result.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write common rule as equation?
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did reason mention reflection swaps x and y?
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you check p≠q gives different result by order?
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.model.0: p=q. Reflection swaps coordinates, but equal movement amounts swap unchanged, so order irrelevant.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.model.1: Like (1,1),(2,2),(−3,−3), vertical/horizontal moves match. Reflection swaps x,y; equal amounts stay same. [1 1 2 2 3 3]
y-m-45-08.s.s3.prompt: Which statement best generalizes s2 to graphs, not one point? [2]
y-m-45-08.s.s3.hint.0: Split p=q vs p≠q; check whether each graph point ends same place in both orders.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.hint.1: Move point (t,−t+c) on line y=−x+c in both orders.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.o.a: Graphs sometimes same/different; if p=q always same.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.r.a: If every point moves to same place, graphs same. If p≠q, some graphs may still coincide.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.o.b: With reflection y=x, swapping translation order always gives same.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.r.b: For p=1,q=2 at (1,3), results differ, so not always. [1 2 1 3]
y-m-45-08.s.s3.o.c: Once translation direction fixed, order does not matter.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.r.c: Direction alone not enough; relation of p,q matters.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.o.d: If p≠q, order always differs for every graph.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.explain: If p=q both orders agree at every point, so same graph. If p≠q usually differ, exception line y=−x+c remains same as y=−x+c+p+q either way.
